title: At the table and eating out
intro: Read plate 6 alongside this unit. The trap to watch is hot: caliente is temperature and picante is spice, and confusing them in a Mexican restaurant has consequences.

entries.note: A deep plate is un plato hondo; el platillo is the saucer.

ex.es: Pon los platos en la mesa.
ex.en: Put the plates on the table.

ex.es: Es el plato típico de la región.
ex.en: It's the region's typical dish.

entries.note: For water or juice, with no stem. Not a vase — that is un florero.

ex.en: Could I have a glass of water?

entries.note: Stemmed. tomar una copa is to go for a drink.

ex.es: Sirvió el vino en copas altas.
ex.en: He served the wine in tall glasses.
Shall we go for a drink?
They won the cup in 2010.

entries.note: For coffee or tea. English cup covers both taza and copa; Spanish keeps them apart.

ex.es: Una taza de café, por favor.
ex.en: A cup of coffee, please.
I dropped my fork.
This knife doesn't cut at all.

entries.note: A teaspoon is una cucharita; a spoonful is una cucharada.

ex.es: Necesito una cuchara para la sopa.
ex.en: I need a spoon for the soup.
Could you bring us more napkins?

ex.es: Pedimos una botella de vino tinto.
ex.en: We ordered a bottle of red wine.

entries.warn: Three unrelated meanings in one word, and none of them is cart. El menú usually means the fixed meal of the day, not the list of dishes — ask for la carta.

ex.en: Could you bring us the menu, please?

ex.es: Le escribí una carta a mi abuela.
ex.en: I wrote my grandmother a letter.

ex.es: Jugamos a las cartas toda la noche.
ex.en: We played cards all night.

entries.note: mesero in Mexico and much of Latin America; mozo in Argentina; camarero in Spain.

ex.es: El mesero nos atendió muy bien.
ex.en: The waiter looked after us very well.

entries.note: Ten per cent is usual in much of Latin America; check whether la propina is already on the bill.

ex.en: Shall we leave a tip?
Drinks are not included.
For dessert I ordered flan.

entries.en: to taste, to try; to try on; to prove

ex.en: Taste the soup, it's really good.
I want to try this shirt on.
Nobody could prove anything.

entries.note: Correct everywhere, but Latin America reaches for tomar in everyday speech. beber leans towards drinking alcohol.

ex.en: That night we drank too much.

entries.note: la cocina is both the kitchen and the cuisine; el cocinero is the cook.

ex.en: He cooks better than any restaurant.

entries.note: Temperature only. For weather Spanish uses hacer calor, not estar caliente.

ex.es: Ten cuidado, el plato está caliente.
ex.en: Be careful, the plate is hot.

entries.warn: English hot means both temperature and spice; Spanish does not. Asking for something caliente when you mean picante will get you warm food, and asking whether the soup is caliente is not asking whether it will burn your mouth.

ex.en: Is the sauce very spicy?

entries.note: tener frío is to feel cold, hacer frío is for the weather, estar frío is for objects. Three different verbs.

ex.en: The soup has gone cold.

ex.es: No aguanto el frío de aquí.
ex.en: I can't stand the cold here.
